newsitem.title: USA: Buckyball nominated as Texas state molecule.
newsitem.headline: Buckyball nominated as Texas state molecule.

text.p: Long before scientists find commercial uses for the buckyball, Texas legislators have a practical application for the revolutionary carbon molecule.

The state legislature is considering making the buckyball, a soccer-ball shaped molecule that won two Texas scientists and a British colleague the Nobel Prize in chemistry, the official state molecule.

"I think it's a real cute idea. It is neat in a sense that it calls attention to part of what Texas thinks its future is -- high tech," Rice University chemist Richard Smalley told Reuters on Thursday.

Smalley and colleagues Robert Curl of Rice and Sir Harold Kroto of the University of Sussex in England were awarded the Nobel Chemistry Prize in October for their chance discovery of the new form of carbon in 1985.
Formally named buckminsterfullerenes after Buckminster Fuller, who designed geodesic domes, buckyballs represent a third known form of carbon along with diamond and graphite.

The first practical applications are expected to be in the form of buckytubes, microthin strands to conduct electricity or be formed into composite materials for superlight bicycles, tennis rackets and airplane wings. But for now, buckyballs likely will join chili, the square dance and the bluebonnet, a wild flower, as symbols of Texas pride.
"I'm actually looking forward to driving into the state from Oklahoma or Louisiana and seeing these signs that say 'Welcome to Texas, home of Buckyball, the state molecule,'" Smalley said.
